messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Khun

Khun was nineteen when his unit came under fire outside a market in Kandahar. He had been in-country for three months, a photographer embedded with a forward patrol, tasked with documenting the work of the soldiers he traveled with. The morning had been routine—dust, heat, the weight of his camera bag, the smell of diesel and sweat. Then the first shots came from the buildings to the north. Khun dropped behind a concrete barrier with the squad leader, a sergeant named Marcus who had become his closest friend in the unit. The firefight lasted seventeen minutes. When it ended, Marcus was dead—a single round through the neck—and Khun was holding his camera, which had recorded everything. He had not moved to help. He had not called for a medic until it was too late. He had done what he was trained to do: document, bear witness, survive. For months afterward, he told himself this was not a failure. It was his role. But the knowing did not stick.

Now, six months home in Portland, Khun had come to believe that he had abandoned Marcus in the moment that mattered most. This conviction—that he should have done something, that he was fundamentally untrustworthy in a crisis—had metastasized into a broader mistrust of himself and others. He was certain that people could not be relied upon, that beneath every interaction lay the possibility of betrayal or indifference. He no longer belonged anywhere. His family's apartment felt foreign; his old friends seemed impossibly naive. When his mother asked how he was sleeping, he heard only the implication that she did not understand him, that she could not possibly. The belief that he had failed when it mattered most had poisoned his sense of safety in the world. He had begun to take risks he knew were dangerous—driving too fast on wet roads, climbing on rooftops for photographs without harnesses, accepting assignments in neighborhoods where violence was common—as if testing whether he deserved to survive at all.

The hypervigilance that had once kept him alive in Kandahar now consumed his civilian life. Every loud noise—a car backfiring, a door slamming, a motorcycle passing—sent him into a state of raw alert, his body braced for incoming fire. He could not relax even in the safety of his apartment with the doors locked. His nervous system had learned that danger was real, imminent, and could arrive without warning. This constant state of threat perception fed directly into his memories of the firefight. When Khun closed his eyes, the seventeen minutes played back with a clarity that eclipsed his ordinary recollections. He could see the exact angle of Marcus's head, the spray of blood against the concrete, the timestamp on the photographs he had taken. The memories felt more real than the present moment—more vivid, more true, more deserving of his attention than anything happening around him now.

When something in his environment triggered the memory—a sound like gunfire, a crowd, the particular quality of afternoon light on a building—the full sensory weight of that day crashed over him without warning. His heart would race, his hands would shake, and he would find himself back in Kandahar, unable to distinguish between what was happening and what had already happened. In these moments, the rage would come. It was a rage directed at himself, at Marcus for dying, at the insurgents, at the world for its casual indifference to suffering. This fury seemed to confirm what he already believed: that he was dangerous, that he could not be trusted, that he did not belong among people who had not experienced what he had. The more he remembered, the more convinced he became that his appraisals were correct—that he was fundamentally compromised, that his failure in that moment had revealed something true and permanent about who he was.

Khun had stopped going to his photography job at a local studio. The enclosed space, the fluorescent lights, the clients' small talk had become intolerable. Instead, he had begun taking freelance assignments—mostly gig work, mostly alone, mostly at night. But even this isolation did not feel safe. He was trapped between the conviction that he could not be trusted in a moment of crisis and the knowledge that his hypervigilance, his startle responses, his constant scanning for threat, were signs that something in him was broken. What had finally brought him to seek help was a moment two weeks ago when his mother found him on the apartment balcony at three in the morning, standing at the edge with no clear plan but a sense of inevitability. She had called a crisis line. Now, sitting in the clinic waiting room, Khun was afraid that talking about any of this would only confirm what he already knew: that he was beyond repair, that the person who had failed to save Marcus was someone who could never be trusted again.
